results.summary: This project implements a Tetris game rendered as a 640x480 at 60 Hz VGA signal. Four inputs (left, right, rotate, down) control the game, and the inputs are expected to be pulled high when idle so that only a low level triggers an action. It requires an external VGA output circuit such as the tiny-vga PMOD to display the picture. The design is notable for fitting a full game into a 2x2 tile area, and the documentation notes that the game-over state can be cleared by pressing the down button a couple of times.

This Wokwi design displays the letters E, L, I, A and S one after another on a 7-segment display, with one second between each letter. It is started with a 10 kHz clock and needs no external hardware beyond the display. The project is explicitly described as only a test so far, and the pin list is incomplete, so little can be said about its inputs. It appears to be an early learning exercise rather than a finished design.

This design animates a snake travelling around a 7-segment display. A chain of flip-flops driven by the clock and reset generates a time sequence, and each step lights the segments that form the moving snake. A step button advances the snake by one tile, and the design uses the 7-segment segments A through G plus the decimal point as outputs. The documentation is brief and the external hardware section is left as an unfilled template, but the behaviour is clear from the description.

This Wokwi project takes two 4-bit numbers on its inputs and adds them, presenting the result on seven outputs. The title and one-line description state that the author does not yet know what the design should do, and the documentation only says that it currently adds two 4-bit numbers. Testing is done by applying two 4-bit values and observing the output, which would normally require switches and a display. The design is a simple arithmetic exercise with minimal documentation.

This design feeds inputs a and b into AND, NAND and OR gates and routes the selected result to the output through control logic, with the state shown on a 7-segment display. A multiplexer select input chooses which logic result is presented, and a truth table in the documentation lists the expected AND, NAND and OR values for each input combination. Testing consists of setting the inputs and verifying the outputs against that table. The project is titled simply test and reads as a basic logic-gate exercise.

This project is described only as an H blinker and provides a single test input and six outputs. There is no explanation of how it works, how to test it, or what external hardware it needs, and the documentation is essentially empty. The title and pin names suggest a simple blinking or pattern generator, but nothing more can be confirmed. It is not possible to describe the design's behaviour in any detail from the available information.

This circuit takes eight digital inputs, passes some through NOT, XOR and AND gates, and drives eight outputs connected to a 7-segment display. Inputs IN0, IN1 and IN2 are tied together as a single signal A that feeds three NOT gates driving OUT0 to OUT2, while IN3 to IN5 pass through directly and IN5 with IN6 feed an XOR and IN6 with IN7 feed an AND. The documentation gives a full output logic table for testing, though the external hardware section is left as an unfilled template. Despite the title RandomNum, the described behaviour is combinational logic rather than a random number generator.

This Wokwi design bundles a full adder, XOR, NAND, AND, D flip-flop and inverter into a single block, with each gate's inputs and outputs brought out to dedicated pins. Inputs 0 and 1 feed the full adder with carry-in tied to ground, inputs 2 and 3 feed the XOR, input 4 feeds the D flip-flop, input 5 feeds the inverter, and inputs 6 and 7 feed the NAND and AND gates. Testing is done with DIP switches to set the gate inputs and a 7-segment display to observe the outputs. The documentation is clear about the wiring but the external hardware section is left as an unfilled template.

This project implements a 4-bit digital lock that asserts an UNLOCK output when the input code equals 1011. Three additional outputs act as Easter eggs for the near-miss codes 1010, 1001 and 0011, and all outputs stay low for any other code. Testing is done by toggling the four input switches and observing LEDs or a 7-segment display against the supplied truth table. The design is a small combinational pattern matcher with clear documentation and no external hardware requirements.

This Wokwi design displays the letter P on a 7-segment display when a secret code is entered on its eight switches. The author started from the template and customised the segment outputs, and the documentation deliberately withholds the code so that users can try to discover it. No external hardware is required beyond the display. The project is a first Wokwi design and is presented as a learning exercise, with the pin names still carrying the template's default labels.
